title: Ice Cream 1.5L

drivers.name: Heatwave (38°C)
drivers.evidence: Historical heat events in Austin show 30% lift in ice cream sales; heatwave forecast for entire week.

drivers.name: Price increase (+2.3%)
drivers.evidence: Past price hikes at similar levels show ~3% demand reduction; no prior promotion at this price.

adjustment.analysis: Thanksgiving week historically shows a slight dip (x0.95 vs baseline), but noise-adjusted effect is x1.0. Price increase to $6.56 (+2.3%) likely suppresses demand. Recent weeks show no promotion, but a heatwave (38°C) is a strong demand driver. Ice cream demand spikes in heat; past heat events show lifts of ~30% in similar stores. The price rise may offset some of this, but heat is more impactful. No prior promotion at this price point. Combine heat (x1.3) and price (x0.97) for net x1.26. Adjust classical model upward. Noise-adjusted evidence supports moderate confidence.

brief:

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: Holiday: Thanksgiving (Thu)
  shelf price: 6.56 (+2.3% vs regular price 6.41)
  planner notes: Heatwave forecast: 38°C all week

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 44.2 | 5%-95%: 11.7 - 74.8 | 10%-90%: 20.3 - 70.4

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-36% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
